summary: Parotitis is inflammation and swelling of the parotid gland. Exam questions ask you to separate viral mumps parotitis from bacterial parotitis using the patient, the duct findings, and the complications, and to explain why salivary stones favor the submandibular gland.

points: Parotid gland is purely serous; its duct (Stensen duct) opens opposite the upper second molar.
Submandibular gland is mixed, mostly serous; its duct (Wharton duct) opens at the sublingual papilla beside the frenulum.
Sublingual gland is mostly mucous and drains by many small ducts into the floor of the mouth.
Parotid secretion is driven by CN IX through the otic ganglion; submandibular and sublingual by CN VII (chorda tympani) through the submandibular ganglion.
Serous cells make salivary amylase, so parotid inflammation raises serum amylase.
notes.why: Serous acini secrete a watery, enzyme-rich fluid, while mucous acini add mucins that make saliva thick, so each gland's mix of acini sets what its saliva is like. Secretion is driven mainly by parasympathetic fibers: CN IX fibers synapse in the otic ganglion and reach the parotid with the auriculotemporal nerve, while CN VII fibers travel in the chorda tympani to the submandibular ganglion. Because the parotid is a major source of salivary amylase, parotid inflammation leaks the salivary isoenzyme into blood and raises total serum amylase while lipase, a pancreatic enzyme, stays normal.

points: Caused by mumps virus, an enveloped negative-sense RNA paramyxovirus spread by respiratory droplets.
Fever and malaise, then painful parotid swelling that is often bilateral (it may start on one side).
Pain with chewing and an earache; the duct opening may be red, but no pus comes out.
Serum amylase is raised from the salivary gland; lipase stays normal unless the pancreas is involved.
Complications: orchitis after puberty (testicular atrophy, rarely sterility), oophoritis, pancreatitis, aseptic meningitis, sensorineural hearing loss.
Prevented by the live attenuated MMR vaccine.
notes.why: Mumps virus replicates first in upper airway epithelium and regional lymph nodes, then spreads by viremia to glandular tissue and the central nervous system. Its hemagglutinin-neuraminidase and fusion proteins let it attach to and infect ductal epithelium, and the resulting interstitial edema with mononuclear cells swells the gland without producing pus at the duct. The same viremic seeding explains orchitis, pancreatitis, and aseptic meningitis. Orchitis matters after puberty because swelling inside the tough, unyielding tunica albuginea causes pressure necrosis of seminiferous tubules and later atrophy.

points: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause.
Low salivary flow lets mouth bacteria climb up Stensen duct.
Risk: dehydration, older age, the days after surgery, poor oral hygiene, anticholinergic drugs, duct obstruction.
Usually one side: hot, red, very tender gland, fever, and leukocytosis.
Massaging the gland pushes pus out of the Stensen duct opening.
Can form an abscess and spread into the deep spaces of the neck.
notes.why: A steady flow of saliva flushes the duct and carries antimicrobial proteins such as lysozyme, lactoferrin, and secretory IgA. When flow falls from dehydration, anticholinergic drugs, or the postoperative state, oral bacteria climb up Stensen duct in a retrograde direction and infect the gland. Neutrophils fill the ducts and acini with pus, so pressure on the gland pushes pus out of the duct opening. The parotid sits inside a tight fascial capsule, which explains the severe pain and why a neglected infection can rupture into the deep neck spaces.

points: About 80 to 90 percent of stones form in the submandibular gland.
Its saliva is thicker (more mucin) and more alkaline, with more calcium and phosphate.
Wharton duct is long and runs upward against gravity, bending around the mylohyoid, so saliva pools.
Stone blocks flow, so the gland swells painfully at meals when secretion is stimulated, then settles.
Stagnant saliva gets infected, causing secondary bacterial sialadenitis.
notes.why: Stones start as a nidus of mucus, shed cells, or debris on which calcium phosphate (mostly hydroxyapatite) precipitates, and submandibular saliva favors this because it is more viscous, more alkaline, and richer in calcium. The anatomy adds stasis, since Wharton duct is long and runs uphill around the posterior border of the mylohyoid. When a meal triggers secretion against a blocked duct, pressure builds behind the stone and the gland swells painfully, then settles as secretion slows. Saliva that sits still loses its flushing effect, so bacteria ascend and cause secondary sialadenitis.

tricks.label: Mumps makes glands as big as POM-POMs
tricks.text: Parotitis, Orchitis, aseptic Meningitis, and Pancreatitis are the classic sites of mumps disease.

tricks.label: Wharton duct flows uphill
tricks.text: Thick saliva that has to climb a long duct against gravity sits still and crystallizes. That is why stones form in the submandibular gland.

tricks.label: Pus means bacteria
tricks.text: If pressing the parotid squeezes pus from the duct opening, think bacterial parotitis. Mumps gives a swollen gland with a clean duct.

highYield: Unvaccinated young adult with bilateral parotid swelling and testicular pain: mumps orchitis.
High serum amylase with normal lipase in mumps comes from the salivary gland.
Older, dehydrated, or postoperative patient with one hot parotid and pus at the duct: Staphylococcus aureus parotitis.
Salivary stones form mostly in the submandibular gland because of thick saliva and an upward duct.
Gland swelling and pain that start with eating point to a duct stone.
Mumps can cause aseptic meningitis with a lymphocytic CSF.
pitfalls: A raised amylase in mumps does not prove pancreatitis; check lipase, which is pancreas-specific.
Mumps can begin on one side, so one-sided swelling does not rule it out; pus at the duct is what points to bacteria.
Stensen duct drains the parotid; Wharton duct drains the submandibular gland.
Stone pain is intermittent and tied to meals; constant pain with fever means the stagnant gland is now infected.

summary: Pancreatitis is the pancreas digesting itself after its enzymes switch on too early. The exam tests the causes, the lab and exam findings of acute pancreatitis, its complications, and how chronic pancreatitis leads to malabsorption and diabetes.

points: Normally trypsinogen is switched on only in the duodenum, by enteropeptidase.
Safeguards: enzymes are made as inactive zymogens, SPINK1 inhibits stray trypsin, and trypsin can destroy itself.
Acinar injury or duct blockage activates trypsin inside the pancreas.
Trypsin then activates phospholipase A2, elastase, and other enzymes, and the gland digests itself.
Results: protein breakdown, fat necrosis, vessel damage with bleeding, and intense inflammation.
notes.why: The pancreas protects itself in layers: enzymes are stored as inactive zymogens in granules kept apart from lysosomes, SPINK1 binds and blocks small amounts of active trypsin, and trypsin can cleave and inactivate itself. Duct obstruction, alcohol, and other insults disturb acinar calcium signaling and let zymogen granules fuse with lysosomes, where cathepsin B converts trypsinogen to trypsin inside the cell. Because trypsin is the activator of the other zymogens, one early step sets off proteolysis, lipolysis, and elastase damage to vessel walls. Injured acinar cells also release cytokines that recruit neutrophils and spread inflammation through the body.

points: Gallstones and alcohol cause most cases.
A gallstone at the ampulla blocks the duct and raises pressure in it.
Hypertriglyceridemia (usually above 1,000 mg/dL) and hypercalcemia (calcium activates trypsinogen).
After ERCP, after blunt abdominal trauma, and with mumps.
Drugs include thiazides, azathioprine, valproate, and sulfonamides.
notes.why: Most causes end at the same step, premature activation of trypsin inside acinar cells. A gallstone at the ampulla raises pressure in the pancreatic duct, while alcohol makes pancreatic juice richer in protein (forming protein plugs), causes spasm of the sphincter of Oddi, and injures acinar cells through its toxic metabolites. Hypercalcemia promotes calcium-dependent activation of trypsinogen and protein plugging. With very high triglycerides, pancreatic lipase releases large amounts of free fatty acids in the pancreatic capillaries, and these fatty acids injure acinar cells and the vessel lining.

points: Sudden epigastric pain boring through to the back, with nausea and vomiting; leaning forward may ease it.
Diagnosis needs two of three: typical pain, lipase or amylase above 3 times the upper limit of normal, typical imaging.
Lipase is more specific than amylase and stays high longer.
Lipase frees fatty acids that bind calcium and form chalky calcium soaps (fat necrosis, saponification).
Calcium used up in soaps causes hypocalcemia, a sign of severe disease.
Cullen sign (periumbilical bruising) and Grey Turner sign (flank bruising) mean blood is tracking from the retroperitoneum.
notes.why: The pancreas lies in the retroperitoneum on the posterior abdominal wall, so its pain is felt in the epigastrium and bores through to the back. Injured acinar cells leak lipase and amylase into blood; lipase comes almost only from the pancreas and is cleared more slowly, which makes it the more specific and longer-lasting test. Lipase in peripancreatic fat releases fatty acids that bind calcium to form insoluble calcium soaps, which lowers serum calcium. When enzymes erode vessel walls, hemorrhagic fluid tracks through retroperitoneal tissue planes to the flank (Grey Turner sign) or toward the umbilicus (Cullen sign).

points: Pseudocyst: enzyme-rich fluid walled off by granulation and fibrous tissue, with no epithelial lining, usually after about 4 weeks.
Pseudocysts can compress nearby organs, rupture, bleed, or become infected.
Necrotic pancreas can become infected by gut bacteria, forming an abscess.
ARDS: circulating enzymes (phospholipase A2 breaks down surfactant) and cytokines injure the lungs.
DIC from release of procoagulant tissue factors into the blood.
Hypovolemic shock from massive fluid loss into the retroperitoneum and from bleeding.
notes.why: Pancreatic juice that escapes a disrupted duct collects in or beside the gland, and the body walls it off with granulation tissue and then fibrous tissue, which is why a pseudocyst has no epithelial lining and takes weeks to mature. Dead pancreatic tissue has no blood supply, so bacteria that cross an injured bowel wall can seed it and cause infected necrosis or an abscess. Systemic complications come from enzymes and cytokines in the circulation: phospholipase A2 and cytokines damage surfactant and the alveolar capillary membrane (ARDS), released tissue factor triggers DIC, and leaky capillaries move large volumes of fluid into the retroperitoneum (hypovolemic shock).

points: Repeated injury causes permanent fibrosis, loss of acini, and strictured, dilated ducts.
Calcifications on imaging are typical, especially with alcohol.
Causes: alcohol in adults, cystic fibrosis (thick secretions plug ducts) in children, duct obstruction.
Hereditary: PRSS1 gain-of-function (trypsin resists inactivation, autosomal dominant) and SPINK1 loss of function.
Exocrine failure (after about 90 percent loss): steatorrhea, weight loss, deficiency of vitamins A, D, E, and K.
Islet loss causes diabetes; lipase and amylase may be normal late in disease.
notes.why: Repeated injury keeps pancreatic stellate cells active, and under TGF-beta they lay down collagen that replaces acini and narrows ducts, while protein plugs inside the ducts calcify. PRSS1 gain-of-function mutations make cationic trypsinogen resist the self-cleavage that normally shuts trypsin off, and SPINK1 loss removes its inhibitor, so both lower the threshold for activation inside the gland. The pancreas has a large reserve, so maldigestion appears only after about 90 percent of exocrine function is gone. Loss of lipase then causes steatorrhea and poor absorption of vitamins A, D, E, and K, and destruction of islets causes pancreatogenic (type 3c) diabetes.

tricks.label: I GET SMASHED
tricks.text: Idiopathic, Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps, Autoimmune, Scorpion sting, Hypercalcemia or Hypertriglyceridemia, ERCP, Drugs (such as thiazides and azathioprine).

tricks.label: Pseudo means no lining
tricks.text: A true cyst is lined by epithelium. A pseudocyst is a walled-off pocket lined only by granulation and fibrous tissue.

tricks.label: Calcium goes into soap
tricks.text: Picture lipase making fatty acids that grab calcium like soap scum. The blood calcium falls as it is locked away in dead fat.

highYield: Epigastric pain to the back plus lipase above 3 times normal: acute pancreatitis.
Gallstones and alcohol are the two leading causes.
Triglycerides above about 1,000 mg/dL can cause pancreatitis.
Low calcium in pancreatitis comes from calcium soap formation in fat necrosis.
Pseudocyst wall is granulation tissue with no epithelium.
Cullen and Grey Turner signs mean retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
PRSS1 mutation makes trypsin resist inactivation, causing hereditary pancreatitis.
Chronic pancreatitis gives steatorrhea, vitamin A, D, E, K deficiency, and diabetes.
pitfalls: Amylase rises in salivary disease and some bowel disorders; lipase is the more specific pancreatic test.
Pseudocyst vs cystic tumor: pseudocyst follows pancreatitis and has no epithelial lining.
In chronic pancreatitis the enzymes may be normal because little gland is left; diagnosis relies on imaging and function.
Hypercalcemia causes pancreatitis, but pancreatitis causes hypocalcemia.

summary: This unit covers the main noninfectious liver diseases: blocked bile flow, inherited bilirubin disorders, alcohol, fatty liver, autoimmune and drug hepatitis, and the cirrhosis and portal hypertension they can lead to. Exam questions give you liver tests and physical signs and ask you to name the process and predict what happens next.

points: Intrahepatic causes: drugs (estrogens, anabolic steroids), pregnancy (third trimester itching), total parenteral nutrition, sepsis, primary biliary cholangitis.
Extrahepatic causes: common bile duct stone, pancreatic head cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, strictures; ultrasound shows dilated ducts.
Labs: conjugated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and GGT rise; GGT confirms the ALP comes from the liver.
Retained bile acids cause itching; high cholesterol causes xanthomas.
No bile reaches the gut: pale stools, dark urine (conjugated bilirubin), poor fat and vitamin K absorption.
notes.why: Bile flow depends on hepatocyte pumps at the canalicular membrane, such as BSEP for bile salts and MRP2 for conjugated bilirubin. Estrogens, pregnancy, sepsis cytokines, some drugs, and TPN cause intrahepatic cholestasis by impairing these pumps, while primary biliary cholangitis destroys the small ducts downstream. Extrahepatic obstruction blocks the large ducts mechanically, so the ducts above the block dilate on ultrasound. In both, conjugated bilirubin backs up into blood and, being water soluble, darkens the urine, bile duct cells make more ALP and GGT, and no bile reaches the gut, so stools turn pale and fat and vitamin K are poorly absorbed.

points: Hepatic stellate (Ito) cells sit in the space of Disse and normally store vitamin A.
Chronic injury releases TGF-beta and other signals that turn stellate cells into collagen-making myofibroblasts.
Collagen in the space of Disse closes sinusoid fenestrations, so exchange with hepatocytes falls.
Bridging fibrous septa and regenerative nodules replace the normal lobules across the whole liver.
Main causes: alcohol, chronic HBV and HCV, fatty liver disease, and metabolic disease (hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency).
notes.why: Resting stellate cells store vitamin A as retinyl esters in the space of Disse. Chronic hepatocyte injury releases reactive oxygen species and signals from Kupffer cells (TGF-beta, PDGF) that turn stellate cells into contractile myofibroblasts, which deposit type I and type III collagen. Collagen in the space of Disse and loss of endothelial fenestrations (capillarization of the sinusoids) block exchange of proteins and solutes between blood and hepatocytes. Fibrous septa then bridge portal tracts and central veins, surviving hepatocytes proliferate into regenerative nodules, and contraction of the myofibroblasts adds to resistance to portal flow.

points: Jaundice from failed conjugation and excretion of bilirubin.
Coagulopathy: the liver makes fewer clotting factors (II, V, VII, IX, X), so PT and INR rise and vitamin K does not correct them.
Low albumin causes edema and adds to ascites.
Poor estrogen breakdown: spider angiomas, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, testicular atrophy.
Hepatic encephalopathy: ammonia escapes the urea cycle and shunts past the liver; confusion and asterixis.
notes.why: Each finding traces back to a hepatocyte function that has been lost. Failed protein synthesis lowers albumin (lower plasma oncotic pressure and edema) and clotting factors, so PT rises and vitamin K cannot correct it because the hepatocytes cannot make the proteins. Failed hepatic breakdown of estrogen, together with more peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogen, causes spider angiomas, palmar erythema, and gynecomastia. Ammonia from gut bacteria escapes the urea cycle and bypasses the liver through portosystemic shunts; in the brain, astrocytes convert it to glutamine and swell, which causes encephalopathy and asterixis.

points: Prehepatic: portal vein thrombosis; varices and splenomegaly with a normal liver.
Intrahepatic: cirrhosis (most common) and schistosomiasis (presinusoidal periportal fibrosis).
Posthepatic: Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis) and right heart failure (nutmeg liver).
Findings: ascites, congestive splenomegaly with low platelets, varices, caput medusae.
notes.why: Portal pressure rises with portal blood flow and with resistance to that flow, and cirrhosis raises both: fibrosis, nodules, and contracting stellate cells raise sinusoidal resistance, while splanchnic vasodilation increases inflow. The site of the block predicts the liver findings: a prehepatic thrombus leaves the liver normal, schistosome eggs cause fibrosis around portal venules before the sinusoids, and posthepatic outflow obstruction congests zone 3 around the central veins (nutmeg liver). Once pressure rises, blood reroutes through portosystemic collaterals (left gastric to esophageal veins, paraumbilical to abdominal wall veins) and backs up into the spleen, which enlarges and traps platelets.

points: Hepatorenal: splanchnic vasodilation lowers effective arterial volume and triggers RAAS and sympathetic drive.
The kidneys clamp down (renal vasoconstriction), so GFR falls and urine sodium is very low, yet the kidneys look normal under the microscope.
Hepatopulmonary: nitric oxide widens lung capillaries, so oxygen cannot diffuse to blood in the middle of the vessel, causing hypoxemia.
Dilations are at the lung bases, so oxygen saturation drops on standing (orthodeoxia).
notes.why: Portal hypertension raises nitric oxide and other vasodilators in the splanchnic circulation, so effective arterial blood volume falls even though total body water is increased. The kidney reads this as hypovolemia: RAAS, sympathetic tone, and ADH constrict renal vessels and retain sodium, so GFR falls while the tubules stay intact, and such kidneys work normally after transplant into a healthy recipient. In the lung, excess nitric oxide dilates capillaries so widely that oxygen cannot diffuse to red cells in the center of the vessel. These dilations are mostly basal, so standing sends more blood through them and saturation falls.

points: Gilbert: mildly reduced UGT1A1; unconjugated bilirubin rises with fasting, stress, illness; benign.
Crigler-Najjar type I: absent UGT1A1; severe unconjugated jaundice and kernicterus in infancy.
Crigler-Najjar type II: partial deficiency, milder; bilirubin falls with phenobarbital, which induces UGT1A1.
Dubin-Johnson: MRP2 defect blocks secretion of conjugated bilirubin; black liver; benign.
Rotor: similar conjugated rise, milder, and the liver is not pigmented.
notes.why: Hepatocytes conjugate bilirubin with glucuronic acid using UGT1A1, then pump the water-soluble conjugate into the canaliculus with MRP2, so the faulty step predicts which fraction rises. A UGT1A1 defect raises unconjugated, lipid-soluble bilirubin, which in severe infant cases crosses into the brain and causes kernicterus. Phenobarbital induces UGT1A1 and helps only when some enzyme exists, so it lowers bilirubin in Crigler-Najjar type II and fails in type I. An MRP2 defect (Dubin-Johnson) traps conjugated bilirubin and pigmented metabolites in hepatocytes and darkens the liver, while Rotor syndrome is a defect in hepatic uptake and storage (OATP1B1 and OATP1B3), so the liver keeps its normal color.

points: Alcohol: steatosis (reversible) to alcoholic hepatitis to cirrhosis.
Alcoholic hepatitis: ballooned hepatocytes, Mallory-Denk bodies (clumped keratin), neutrophils; AST to ALT ratio above 2.
MASLD: insulin resistance and obesity flood the liver with fatty acids; ALT usually above AST.
Simple steatosis is fat only; MASH adds inflammation and ballooning and can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
Autoimmune hepatitis: young women, high IgG, ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody, interface hepatitis with plasma cells.
Acetaminophen overdose: CYP2E1 makes NAPQI, glutathione runs out, zone 3 (centrilobular) necrosis; N-acetylcysteine replaces glutathione.
Isoniazid causes hepatitis that is more common with older age and alcohol use.
notes.why: Alcohol metabolism by alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases generates excess NADH, which blocks fatty acid oxidation and favors triglyceride synthesis (steatosis), while acetaldehyde and free radicals from CYP2E1 damage hepatocytes and their keratin cytoskeleton (Mallory-Denk bodies). AST exceeds ALT in alcohol injury because alcohol damages mitochondria, which hold much of the AST, and vitamin B6 deficiency lowers ALT activity more. In MASLD, insulin resistance increases delivery of fatty acids to the liver, and lipotoxicity and oxidative stress turn steatosis into steatohepatitis. Acetaminophen injures zone 3 because CYP2E1 is concentrated around the central vein, where NAPQI forms once glutathione is used up.

tricks.label: ToAST
tricks.text: In alcoholic liver disease AST runs higher than ALT, usually more than twice as high. Picture the liver toasted by alcohol.

tricks.label: Dubin-Johnson is dark
tricks.text: Dubin-Johnson makes the liver black. Rotor is the look-alike with a normal colored liver.

tricks.label: Before, in, after the liver
tricks.text: Sort portal hypertension by following blood: portal vein (before), sinusoids (in), hepatic veins and right heart (after).

tricks.label: Gilbert skips breakfast
tricks.text: A healthy person who turns slightly yellow after fasting or a cold, with normal liver enzymes and no hemolysis, has Gilbert syndrome.

highYield: Middle-aged woman, itching, high ALP, antimitochondrial antibody: primary biliary cholangitis.
Ulcerative colitis with beaded bile ducts: primary sclerosing cholangitis, with cholangiocarcinoma risk.
Stellate cells in the space of Disse make the collagen of cirrhosis.
Spider angiomas, palmar erythema, and gynecomastia come from high estrogen in liver failure.
Asterixis and confusion in cirrhosis: hepatic encephalopathy from ammonia.
Hepatorenal syndrome: kidney failure with very low urine sodium and normal kidney histology.
Acetaminophen overdose injures zone 3 first; N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione.
Mallory-Denk bodies plus AST to ALT above 2: alcoholic hepatitis.
pitfalls: Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar raise unconjugated bilirubin; Dubin-Johnson and Rotor raise conjugated bilirubin.
High PT from cholestasis corrects with vitamin K; high PT from liver failure does not.
PBC damages small intrahepatic ducts; PSC damages large and small ducts with beading.
Budd-Chiari is posthepatic (hepatic veins); portal vein thrombosis is prehepatic.
MASLD has ALT higher than AST; alcohol has AST higher than ALT.

flows.title: Cirrhosis: injury to nodules
steps: Chronic injury from alcohol, viral hepatitis, or fatty liver damages hepatocytes
Kupffer cells release TGF-beta, PDGF, and reactive oxygen species

summary: Gallstones are common, and where a stone ends up decides the disease it causes. The exam tests stone types and risk factors, acute cholecystitis and its calculous and acalculous forms, and complications such as cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis, gallstone ileus, and Mirizzi syndrome.

points: Bile salts and lecithin hold cholesterol in micelles.
Cholesterol stones form when bile has too much cholesterol or too few bile salts, plus gallbladder stasis.
Cholesterol stone risks: female sex, obesity, pregnancy, estrogen or oral contraceptives, rapid weight loss, older age, fibrates.
Estrogen increases cholesterol secretion into bile; progesterone slows gallbladder emptying.
Black pigment stones (calcium bilirubinate) form with chronic hemolysis such as sickle cell disease and hereditary spherocytosis.
Brown pigment stones form in infected bile ducts: bacterial beta-glucuronidase frees unconjugated bilirubin.
notes.why: Cholesterol is insoluble in water and stays dissolved only in micelles and vesicles made with bile salts and lecithin, so stones begin when cholesterol exceeds that capacity (supersaturation), crystals nucleate, and a slow gallbladder holds them long enough to grow. Estrogen increases cholesterol uptake by the liver and its secretion into bile, obesity and rapid weight loss increase cholesterol output, and fibrates inhibit cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme that converts cholesterol into bile acids. Pigment stones follow the bilirubin supply: hemolysis floods bile with bilirubin that precipitates as calcium bilirubinate (black stones), and bacterial beta-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin in infected ducts (brown stones).

notes.h: Where the stone goes, what it causes
points: In the gallbladder: often silent.
Brief block of the cystic duct: biliary colic, pain after a fatty meal (CCK makes the gallbladder contract) that settles within hours, normal labs.
Stuck in the cystic duct: acute cholecystitis.
In the common bile duct (choledocholithiasis): obstructive jaundice with high conjugated bilirubin and ALP.
Common duct stone plus infection: ascending cholangitis with fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain (Charcot triad).
At the ampulla: gallstone pancreatitis.
Through a cholecystoenteric fistula: gallstone ileus, small bowel obstruction usually at the ileocecal valve, with air in the biliary tree.
notes.why: A cystic duct block isolates only the gallbladder, so bile still drains from the liver and bilirubin and ALP stay normal; CCK released by fatty chyme makes the gallbladder contract against the stone and causes colic. A common bile duct stone blocks the whole biliary tree, so conjugated bilirubin and ALP rise, and stagnant bile lets gut bacteria ascend and cause cholangitis; at the ampulla the stone can also block the pancreatic duct. A large stone that erodes through the gallbladder wall into the bowel lodges at the narrowest point, the ileocecal valve, and the fistula lets air into the bile ducts.

points: Calculous: a stone stays stuck in the cystic duct and the gallbladder distends.
First chemical inflammation (lysolecithin and prostaglandins irritate the wall), then bacterial infection by gut organisms such as E. coli.
Right upper quadrant pain lasting more than about 6 hours, fever, leukocytosis.
Murphy sign: the patient stops breathing in when the examiner presses under the right costal margin.
Acalculous: no stone; occurs in critically ill patients (sepsis, burns, trauma, major surgery, TPN) from stasis and ischemia.
Acalculous disease has a higher risk of gangrene and perforation.
notes.why: When the stone stays in the cystic duct, trapped bile distends the gallbladder, and phospholipase from injured mucosa converts lecithin to toxic lysolecithin, which with prostaglandins strips the protective mucus and inflames the wall. Rising pressure in the distended organ reduces blood flow to its wall, and enteric bacteria then infect it. When the inflamed wall touches the parietal peritoneum, pain becomes sharp and localized, and the descending gallbladder meeting the examiner's hand stops inspiration (Murphy sign). Acalculous disease arises from stasis (fasting, TPN, opioids, no CCK stimulus) and poor perfusion in critically ill patients, which is why gangrene and perforation are more likely.

points: Repeated attacks scar and thicken the gallbladder wall.
Calcium deposits in the scarred wall give a porcelain gallbladder.
Porcelain gallbladder and long-standing gallstones raise the risk of gallbladder adenocarcinoma.
notes.why: Repeated bouts of obstruction and inflammation, almost always with stones, cause fibrosis and a thick, contracted wall that empties poorly. Dystrophic calcification in this scarred wall produces the porcelain gallbladder. Long-standing mucosal irritation from stones and inflammation drives a sequence of metaplasia, dysplasia, and carcinoma, which is why gallstones are the main risk factor for gallbladder adenocarcinoma. That cancer causes few symptoms early, so it is usually found only after it invades the liver or bile ducts.

points: A stone stuck in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck presses on the common hepatic duct from outside.
Result: obstructive jaundice even though no stone sits in the common bile duct.
notes.why: The cystic duct and common hepatic duct run close together, sometimes side by side for a long distance, before they join. A large stone impacted in the gallbladder neck (Hartmann pouch) or cystic duct, along with the inflammation around it, presses on the common hepatic duct from outside and narrows it. Bile from the liver cannot pass, so the patient has conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and raised ALP that mimic a common duct stone, although the common bile duct itself is clear. Long-standing pressure can erode into the duct and form a cholecystocholedochal fistula.

tricks.label: The 4 Fs
tricks.text: Female, Fat (obese), Fertile (pregnancy, multiparity), Forty: classic risk factors for cholesterol gallstones.

tricks.label: Black is blood, brown is bugs
tricks.text: Black pigment stones come from hemolysis. Brown pigment stones come from bacteria or parasites in the bile ducts.

tricks.label: Add one finding, change one diagnosis
tricks.text: Pain under 6 hours with normal labs is biliary colic. Pain over 6 hours with fever and leukocytosis is cholecystitis. Jaundice points to a stone in the common bile duct, and fever with jaundice and right upper quadrant pain is cholangitis.

highYield: Charcot triad (fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain) means ascending cholangitis.
Reynolds pentad adds hypotension and confusion to Charcot triad.
Air in the biliary tree with small bowel obstruction in an older woman: gallstone ileus.
Critically ill patient with gallbladder inflammation and no stones: acalculous cholecystitis.
Porcelain gallbladder is linked to gallbladder adenocarcinoma.
Hemolytic anemia in a child with gallstones: black pigment stones.
Mirizzi syndrome causes jaundice from outside compression of the common hepatic duct.
pitfalls: Biliary colic lasts a few hours with normal labs; cholecystitis lasts longer with fever and leukocytosis.
Plain cholecystitis rarely causes marked jaundice; jaundice suggests a duct stone, cholangitis, or Mirizzi syndrome.
Gallstone ileus is a mechanical obstruction of the small bowel, usually at the ileocecal valve.
Black stones form in the gallbladder; brown stones form in the bile ducts.

summary: Malabsorption happens when food is not broken down (enzyme or acid problems) or not taken up by a damaged or bypassed bowel. The exam asks you to match the stool, the labs, and the vitamin pattern to the cause: achlorhydria, celiac disease, pancreatic or brush border enzyme loss, lactase deficiency, short bowel, or bacterial overgrowth.

points: Causes: autoimmune atrophic gastritis (antibodies to parietal cells and intrinsic factor), chronic H. pylori pangastritis with atrophy, gastrectomy.
No acid means no feedback on antral G cells, so gastrin rises.
Gastrin drives ECL cell hyperplasia, which can progress to gastric carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumors.
Iron needs acid to stay soluble and reduced (Fe2+), so iron deficiency follows.
Acid and pepsin free B12 from food; autoimmune gastritis also loses intrinsic factor, causing pernicious anemia.
Without the acid barrier, bacteria overgrow in the stomach and small bowel.
notes.why: Gastric acid normally limits its own stimulus, because low antral pH releases somatostatin from D cells, which restrains G cells. When parietal cells in the body and fundus are lost (autoimmune attack on the H+/K+ ATPase, or atrophy from long-standing H. pylori) and the antrum is left in place, pH stays high, somatostatin falls, and G cells release gastrin without a brake. Gastrin is trophic to ECL cells, so they proliferate and can form type 1 gastric carcinoids. Acid also keeps dietary iron soluble in the ferrous (Fe2+) form, frees B12 from food proteins, and kills swallowed bacteria, which explains iron deficiency, B12 deficiency, and bacterial overgrowth.

points: Tissue transglutaminase deamidates gliadin, which binds HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 and activates CD4 T cells.
Biopsy: villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, more intraepithelial lymphocytes.
Worst in the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum, where iron and folate are absorbed.
Iron deficiency anemia that does not respond to oral iron is a common first sign.
Antibodies: IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase and antiendomysial; check total IgA because IgA deficiency is linked.
Dermatitis herpetiformis: itchy vesicles on elbows and knees with IgA in the dermal papillae.
Long-term risk of enteropathy-associated T cell lymphoma.
notes.why: Gliadin peptides are rich in proline and glutamine, resist digestion, and cross the epithelium, where tissue transglutaminase converts glutamine residues to glutamate. The added negative charge lets these peptides bind HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 tightly, so antigen-presenting cells activate gluten-specific CD4 T cells that release interferon-gamma, while IL-15 from stressed epithelium arms intraepithelial CD8 lymphocytes to kill enterocytes. Villi are lost faster than crypts can replace them, so crypts lengthen while absorptive surface shrinks, and damage is worst proximally where gluten exposure is greatest and where iron and folate are absorbed. Chronic activation of intraepithelial lymphocytes explains the risk of enteropathy-associated T cell lymphoma.

points: Pancreatic insufficiency (chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis) blocks digestion of fat and protein: steatorrhea, weight loss, low vitamins A, D, E, K.
Fecal elastase is low in pancreatic insufficiency.
D-xylose needs no digestion, so it tests the mucosa: normal in pancreatic disease, low in mucosal disease such as celiac.
Enteropeptidase (brush border) normally activates trypsinogen; congenital deficiency stops all protease activation.
Enteropeptidase deficiency causes protein malabsorption in infants: diarrhea, failure to thrive, low protein, edema.
notes.why: Digestion and absorption are separate steps: pancreatic enzymes break fats and proteins into absorbable pieces in the lumen, and the mucosa then absorbs them. D-xylose is a sugar absorbed without any digestion, so its level in blood and urine tests only the mucosa, while fecal elastase, a pancreatic enzyme that survives transit, tests only pancreatic output. Enteropeptidase sits at the top of the protease cascade: it cleaves trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, and procarboxypeptidases. Losing that single brush border enzyme disables every pancreatic protease and causes protein malabsorption with low plasma protein and edema.

points: Primary (adult type): lactase falls after childhood; common in people of East Asian, African, and Native American ancestry; villi are normal.
Secondary: villus tips are injured, as after viral enteritis or in celiac disease.
Unabsorbed lactose pulls water into the gut: osmotic diarrhea with a high stool osmotic gap and acidic stool.
Colon bacteria ferment lactose to gas and acids: bloating, cramps, flatulence after dairy.
Hydrogen breath test rises after a lactose load; diarrhea stops with fasting.
notes.why: Lactase sits at the tips of the villi, the most exposed position, so mucosal injury such as viral enteritis or celiac disease lowers it first; in primary deficiency, a genetically programmed fall in lactase after weaning leaves the villi normal. Undigested lactose is osmotically active and holds water in the lumen, so the stool osmotic gap is high and diarrhea stops when the patient fasts. Colon bacteria ferment lactose into short-chain fatty acids, which acidify the stool, and into gases including hydrogen. The hydrogen is absorbed into blood and exhaled, which is what the breath test measures.

points: Short bowel after extensive resection: watery diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss.
Losing the terminal ileum loses B12 uptake and bile acid recycling, so B12 deficiency and fat malabsorption follow.
Unabsorbed fat binds calcium, leaving oxalate free to be absorbed in the colon: calcium oxalate kidney stones.
Blind loop after gastric surgery (stasis) lets bacteria overgrow.
Bacteria deconjugate bile acids (micelles fail, steatorrhea) and consume B12, while making folate (normal or high folate).
notes.why: The terminal ileum carries the receptor for B12 bound to intrinsic factor and the sodium-dependent bile acid transporter. Losing it breaks enterohepatic recycling, and when the liver cannot replace the lost bile acids the micelle pool shrinks and fat is malabsorbed. In the lumen, fatty acids bind calcium to form soaps, so oxalate that would normally precipitate as insoluble calcium oxalate stays soluble and is absorbed by a remaining colon, then filtered by the kidney to form stones. In a blind loop, anaerobes deconjugate bile acids, which are absorbed early in the jejunum, take up B12 before the ileum can absorb it, and synthesize folate.

tricks.label: D-xylose skips digestion
tricks.text: D-xylose is absorbed without enzymes, so it only tests the bowel wall. Low result means mucosal disease (or bacteria eating it); normal result points to the pancreas.

tricks.label: Bacteria eat B12 and make folate
tricks.text: In bacterial overgrowth B12 falls and folate stays normal or rises. Two vitamins moving in opposite directions is the clue.

tricks.label: Tips go first
tricks.text: Lactase sits at the villus tips, so any mucosal injury (viral enteritis, celiac) knocks it out first.

highYield: Autoimmune gastritis: achlorhydria, high gastrin, pernicious anemia, and carcinoid risk.
Celiac disease: villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytes, worst in distal duodenum.
Iron deficiency anemia not fixed by oral iron should prompt testing for celiac disease.
Dermatitis herpetiformis is a skin sign of celiac disease.

Bloating and diarrhea after dairy with normal villi: primary lactase deficiency.
Ileal resection leads to B12 deficiency, bile acid loss, and calcium oxalate stones.
Blind loop: low B12 with normal or high folate.
pitfalls: Pernicious anemia lacks intrinsic factor; bacterial overgrowth has intrinsic factor but bacteria use up the B12.
Primary lactase deficiency has normal villi; secondary lactase deficiency follows mucosal injury.
Oxalate stones after bowel resection need the colon to be present, because oxalate is absorbed there.
Celiac IgA tests can be falsely negative in IgA deficiency, so total IgA is checked.

summary: This unit covers disorders that block or stall movement through the gut, from the esophagus to the rectum. The exam asks you to tell a nerve or muscle failure (achalasia, ileus, Hirschsprung disease) from a mechanical block (hernia, intussusception, volvulus) and to predict the findings and complications of each.

points: Achalasia: loss of inhibitory (nitric oxide and VIP) neurons in the myenteric plexus.
Result: the LES cannot relax and the distal esophagus loses peristalsis.
Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start, regurgitation, weight loss.
Barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus tapering to a bird beak; manometry shows incomplete LES relaxation and no peristalsis.
Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) destroys the plexus and causes secondary achalasia.
Zenker diverticulum: a false diverticulum (mucosa and submucosa) pushing out above the cricopharyngeus.
Cricopharyngeal dysfunction raises pressure; regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, aspiration in older adults.
notes.why: Swallowing normally triggers release of nitric oxide and VIP from inhibitory myenteric neurons, which relaxes the LES and creates the descending wave of inhibition that coordinates peristalsis. When these neurons are lost (idiopathic and possibly autoimmune in primary achalasia, or from Trypanosoma cruzi in Chagas disease), excitatory cholinergic input is unopposed, so the LES stays closed and the esophageal body loses peristalsis, with dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start. Zenker diverticulum forms because a cricopharyngeus that fails to open fully raises pressure during swallowing, pushing mucosa and submucosa out through Killian triangle, a weak area between the thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal parts of the inferior constrictor.

points: Adynamic (paralytic) ileus: the bowel stops moving with no physical block.
Causes: abdominal surgery, peritonitis, hypokalemia, opioids.
Adynamic signs: distension, absent bowel sounds, gas spread through small and large bowel.
Mechanical obstruction causes: adhesions (most common in the small bowel), hernias, tumors, impaction.
Mechanical signs: colicky pain, vomiting, high-pitched bowel sounds early, dilated loops above a transition point with little gas below.
notes.why: Normal motility needs working enteric neurons, excitable smooth muscle, and balanced autonomic input. After abdominal surgery or with peritonitis, sympathetic inhibitory reflexes and inflammatory mediators suppress motility; hypokalemia hyperpolarizes smooth muscle; and opioids act on mu receptors in the enteric plexus to stop propulsion, so the whole bowel goes quiet and gas spreads evenly. In mechanical obstruction the bowel above the block contracts harder to push contents past it, producing colicky pain and high-pitched sounds, while the bowel beyond the block empties, which creates the transition point on imaging. As the obstructed bowel tires and distends, sounds fade and wall tension can compromise blood flow.

points: Sliding hiatal hernia: the GE junction slides up into the chest; most common type; linked to reflux.
Paraesophageal hiatal hernia: GE junction stays in place and the fundus rolls up beside the esophagus; can incarcerate or strangulate.
Incarcerated hernia: bowel is trapped and cannot be pushed back.
Strangulation: the tight neck squeezes thin-walled veins first, then swelling raises pressure until arterial inflow stops and the bowel infarcts.
Femoral hernias have the highest risk of strangulation.
notes.why: A sliding hiatal hernia moves the GE junction above the diaphragm, which removes the support of the crural diaphragm and the abdominal segment of the LES, so reflux follows. In a paraesophageal hernia the junction stays anchored and the fundus herniates beside the esophagus, where it can twist or be pinched. Strangulation follows a pressure sequence: the hernia neck first compresses thin-walled, low-pressure veins while arterial inflow continues, so the trapped bowel swells with edema until tissue pressure exceeds arterial pressure and the bowel infarcts. Femoral hernias carry the highest risk because the femoral ring is narrow and bounded by unyielding ligaments (inguinal, lacunar, and pectineal).

points: Intussusception: one segment telescopes into the next, most often ileocolic in children about 6 months to 3 years old.
Lead points: hypertrophied Peyer patches after viral infection, Meckel diverticulum, polyps; in adults, a tumor.
Findings: bouts of colicky pain with legs drawn up, sausage-shaped mass, currant jelly stool (mucosal ischemia), target sign on ultrasound.
Volvulus: bowel twists on its mesentery, blocking the lumen and its blood supply.
Sigmoid volvulus is most common in older adults with chronic constipation (coffee bean sign).
Midgut volvulus occurs in infants with malrotation and presents with bilious vomiting.
notes.why: Peristalsis grabs a lead point, such as Peyer patches enlarged after an adenovirus infection or a Meckel diverticulum, and pulls it with its mesentery into the bowel ahead. The trapped mesentery is squeezed, so venous outflow is blocked first, and congested, ischemic mucosa sheds blood and mucus that form currant jelly stool. In volvulus, a loop rotates around its mesenteric axis and blocks the lumen and the mesenteric vessels at the same time, producing a closed-loop obstruction with early ischemia. Sigmoid volvulus needs a long, redundant sigmoid on a narrow mesenteric base, and malrotation leaves the midgut on a narrow base around the superior mesenteric artery.

points: Hirschsprung disease: neural crest cells fail to migrate, so ganglion cells are missing from the rectum and a continuous segment above it.
The aganglionic segment stays contracted; colon above it dilates.
Newborn fails to pass meconium within 48 hours, distended abdomen, empty rectal vault, then explosive stool after a rectal exam.
Linked to RET mutations and Down syndrome; diagnosed by rectal suction biopsy.
Chagas disease destroys the myenteric plexus later in life (acquired megacolon and megaesophagus).
Toxic megacolon: acute colon dilation with systemic toxicity complicating ulcerative colitis or C. difficile colitis; risk of perforation.
notes.why: Enteric neurons come from neural crest cells that migrate down the gut from the cranial end to the caudal end, so a failure of migration (often from loss-of-function RET mutations) always leaves the rectum aganglionic and extends upward as one continuous segment. Without the inhibitory neurons of the myenteric and submucosal plexuses, that segment cannot relax and acts as a functional obstruction, so the normal colon above it dilates. Chagas disease does the same in adults by destroying plexus neurons. Toxic megacolon instead comes from inflammation that extends into the muscle layer and paralyzes it, partly through nitric oxide, so the thin, dilated wall can perforate.

points: Gastroparesis: delayed gastric emptying with no blockage, most often from diabetic autonomic (vagal) neuropathy.
Gastroparesis symptoms: early satiety, nausea, vomiting of undigested food hours after meals, bloating.
Irritable bowel syndrome: recurrent abdominal pain linked to defecation and a change in stool frequency or form.
IBS has no structural disease; weight loss, bleeding, or anemia suggest another diagnosis.
notes.why: Gastric emptying depends on vagal coordination of fundic relaxation, antral contractions, and pyloric opening, so diabetic autonomic neuropathy, often with loss of interstitial cells of Cajal, slows emptying and leaves food in the stomach for hours. IBS is a disorder of gut-brain interaction: visceral hypersensitivity, altered motility, changes in the gut microbiome, and altered central pain processing produce pain linked to defecation with no structural lesion. Because nothing is structurally damaged, weight loss, bleeding, anemia, or symptoms that wake the patient at night point toward organic disease.

tricks.label: A-chalasia means no relaxing
tricks.text: Chalasia means relaxation. Achalasia is the LES that cannot relax because its nitric oxide neurons are gone.

tricks.label: Solids first or both at once
tricks.text: A mechanical narrowing (stricture, cancer) blocks solids first. A motility problem like achalasia blocks solids and liquids from the start.

tricks.label: Veins before arteries
tricks.text: In strangulation, soft veins collapse first, the bowel swells, and only then are the arteries squeezed shut. That is why trapped bowel turns dark and swollen before it dies.

highYield: Bird-beak esophagus with dysphagia to solids and liquids: achalasia.
Achalasia in a patient from Latin America: think Chagas disease.
Older adult with halitosis and regurgitation of old food: Zenker diverticulum.
Absent bowel sounds after surgery or with low potassium: adynamic ileus.
Currant jelly stool and a sausage-shaped mass in a toddler: intussusception.
Coffee bean sign in an older constipated patient: sigmoid volvulus.
Newborn with no meconium by 48 hours and an empty rectum: Hirschsprung disease.
Diabetic with early satiety and vomiting of food eaten hours ago: gastroparesis.
pitfalls: Hirschsprung always involves the rectum; the dilated part is the normal colon above the aganglionic segment.
Zenker is a false diverticulum (no muscle layer); Meckel diverticulum is a true diverticulum.
A sliding hernia moves the GE junction up; a paraesophageal hernia leaves it in place.
Ileus has diffuse gas with no transition point; mechanical obstruction has a transition point.

dumps.p: Make a table comparing adynamic ileus, intussusception, volvulus, and strangulated hernia. Include cause, typical patient, and key findings.
l: Adynamic ileus: surgery, peritonitis, hypokalemia, opioids
Adynamic ileus: absent bowel sounds, diffuse gas
Intussusception: ileocolic in young children with a lead point
Intussusception: currant jelly stool, sausage mass, target sign
Volvulus: sigmoid in older adults, midgut with malrotation in infants
Strangulation: venous block, then swelling, then arterial block and infarction
Mechanical obstruction: high-pitched bowel sounds and a transition point

dumps.p: Draw the gut wall layers and label the myenteric and submucosal plexuses. Then show what goes wrong in achalasia, Hirschsprung disease, Chagas disease, and gastroparesis.
l: Myenteric plexus lies between the muscle layers; submucosal plexus in the submucosa
Achalasia: loss of nitric oxide and VIP inhibitory neurons
Achalasia: LES fails to relax, no peristalsis, bird beak
Hirschsprung: neural crest migration failure, no ganglion cells in rectum
Hirschsprung: delayed meconium, empty rectal vault
Chagas: Trypanosoma cruzi destroys the plexus, megaesophagus and megacolon
Gastroparesis: diabetic vagal neuropathy slows gastric emptying

videos.title: Achalasia (esophageal) - signs and symptoms, pathophysiology, investigations and treatment

flows.title: Achalasia
steps: Inhibitory myenteric neurons are lost (idiopathic or Trypanosoma cruzi)
Nitric oxide and VIP release falls
LES fails to relax and the esophageal body loses peristalsis
Food and liquid pool above the closed LES
Esophagus dilates and tapers to a bird beak on barium swallow

flows.title: Hernia strangulation
steps: Bowel herniates through a narrow neck and becomes incarcerated
The neck compresses thin-walled veins while arteries still fill
Venous congestion causes bowel wall edema
Tissue pressure rises until arterial inflow stops
Ischemia progresses to infarction, gangrene, and perforation

flows.title: Hirschsprung disease
steps: Neural crest cells fail to complete migration down the gut, often from RET mutation
Rectum and a continuous segment above it lack ganglion cells
Aganglionic segment cannot relax and stays contracted
Stool cannot pass: functional obstruction
Proximal colon dilates; meconium is delayed beyond 48 hours
